atoms.text: Britain’s slave trade was part of a wider Atlantic system linking Britain and Europe, West Africa, North America and the West Indies (Caribbean).
atoms.sound: Britain’s slave trade was part of a wider Atlantic system linking Britain and Europe, West Africa, North America, and the West Indies, which are islands in the Caribbean.

atoms.a: Britain and other European countries set up fortresses along the West African coast. Through them, traders and military enforced the enslavement of African people by influencing and amplifying local conflicts and exchanging goods.

Over 12 million enslaved Africans were transported via slave ships to America. In the growing plantation system, they produced tobacco, rice and cotton. In the British West Indies, the economy was highly dependent on slave labour, with places such as Jamaica and Barbados being organised around large sugar plantations.

The produce from the plantations was shipped to Britain and Europe. Tobacco, tea, sugar and rum were sold as exotic goods to the growing middle class. Cotton was processed into fabric and became central in the clothing market. Machines to process cotton stood at the core of Britain's industrial development.
